source: Rønnow et al. (2014), Defining and detecting quantum speedup, Science 345(6195), 420–424. DOI 10.1126/science.1252319
role: Benchmark-validity anchor: polices whether an advantage/speedup/supremacy claim is well-defined and whether the classical comparator is fair
currency_note: Old but still primary; later benchmark-standard papers refine reporting practice rather than replacing the taxonomy

speedup_taxonomy._note: Rønnow Section II.B defines five types of quantum speedup. The type determines how stringent the validity bar is.
speedup_taxonomy.provable: Proven no classical algorithm can outperform the quantum one (e.g., Grover lower bound)
speedup_taxonomy.strong: Compared against the best possible classical algorithm (unknown for most problems)
speedup_taxonomy.quantum: Compared against the best available classical algorithm (community-dependent)
speedup_taxonomy.potential: Compared against a specific classical algorithm or set of algorithms
speedup_taxonomy.limited: Compared against a 'corresponding' classical algorithm implementing the same approach on classical hardware (e.g., SA vs QA)

speedup_claim_present.description: Experiment or paper must make an explicit advantage, speedup, or supremacy claim

classical_baseline_identified.description: A specific classical algorithm or method must be named as the comparator — not just 'brute force' or unspecified. Per Rønnow: 'one must make a genuine attempt to compare against the best classical algorithms known' (Section II.B, potential speedup).

comparison_type_defined.description: The speedup must be classifiable by Rønnow's taxonomy: is it provable, strong, quantum (vs best available), potential (vs specific algorithm), or limited (vs corresponding classical analogue)? At minimum, it must be clear whether the comparison is algorithmic or empirical.

optimal_parameters.description: Per Rønnow Section IV.A: the comparison must use optimal or near-optimal parameters for BOTH the quantum and classical sides. Fixed or suboptimal annealing times can fake or mask speedup. The 'true scaling' requires size-dependent optimization of parameters.

hardware_resource_parity.description: Per Rønnow Section IV.B (Eq. 4–5): classical and quantum hardware resources must scale comparably. A quantum device using N qubits should be compared against a classical device with O(N) equivalent resources, not a single core. Otherwise a parallel speedup may be mistaken for a quantum speedup.

instance_fairness.description: Per Rønnow Section V: comparison must use representative instances, not cherry-picked favorable subsets. The paper distinguishes 'ratio of quantiles' (aggregate performance on hardest cases) from 'quantile of ratios' (instance-by-instance). Aggregate comparison on the full dataset is the stronger test.

scaling_evidence.description: For asymptotic claims, at least two problem sizes should be tested to show scaling behavior. Per Rønnow Fig. 1: the apparent scaling at fixed annealing time is misleading — only the envelope of optimal parameters reveals true scaling.

well_defined_claim.conditions: Speedup claimed, classical baseline named, comparison type clear, no instance-fairness or parameter-optimization red flags

claim_with_weak_baseline.conditions: Speedup claimed but classical baseline is weak, generic, or unspecified

claim_without_type.conditions: Speedup claimed but comparison type not defined (Rønnow taxonomy unclear)

claim_with_fairness_concerns.conditions: Speedup claimed but instance selection or parameter optimization raises concerns

no_claim.conditions: No explicit advantage/speedup/supremacy claim made — framework does not apply

undefined_speedup.conditions: Advantage claimed but cannot be meaningfully interpreted: no baseline, no metric, no comparison
